It may be said that its position is automatic and does not have any semantic role. Due to its non-phonemicity, there are no contrasting levels of stress. It is so non-significant that the presence or absence or position does not alter the sense of any morphemes (Chatterjee, 1921-19). new_statements.quote: Stress is not phonemic in either SCB and ND as it does not exist with contrasts on the position of intensity. It may be said that its position is automatic and does not have any semantic role. [...] Both in SCB and ND stress is predictable mostly for the inflected morphemes where it is always placed on the initial syllable. [...] Though word stress is always subsidiary to sentence-stress, there are few exceptions to this rule. Chatterjee (1921-19) shows that conjunctions, particles, auxiliaries in compound verbs do not receive any stress. If any noun follows an adjective it loses the stress, which falls on the adjective.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress in the Noakhali dialect (ND) is non-contrastive and automatic: it falls on the initial syllable of the word, and at phrase level on the initial syllable of the first content word of the sense-group, all other words losing their stress. Morshed's ND examples mark the first syllable of the utterance: ['dʒɔr oiʃe] 'I got fever', ['adʒ ki kirum] 'what shall I do to-day?', ['he balai kam kɔre] 'he got a good job'. Haldar 1929 (pp. 28-29) independently reaches the same conclusion for Noakhali ('the initial word-stress prevails just as in the Standard Colloquial speech'), with word-level evidence from the lengthening of initial vowels and the elision or shortening of the vowel of the following syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described. Morshed: 'there are no contrasting levels of stress'; only an emphatic stress (tenser consonants, lengthened vowels over a syllable) exists besides the automatic initial stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Morshed: conjunctions, particles and the auxiliary of compound verbs are unstressed; a noun following an adjective loses its stress to the adjective (both after Chatterji 1921). Haldar 1929: in Persian/Arabic loans 'the stress is thrown back' (i.e. still initial, cf. LSI V-1); his sec. 58 notes 'puzzles' -- extended name forms like [ɦasoinna] 'Hasan', [khitta] 'Kshitisa' where the dialect resists the vowel modification that strong initial stress produces in Standard Bengali -- but he still holds initial stress to prevail in connected speech.
new_statements.domain_note: Both sources treat stress as primarily a sentence/sense-group phenomenon with word stress 'subsidiary to sentence-stress'; Morshed's ND examples are short sentences, not isolated citation forms, and his statement is framed as holding for both Standard Colloquial Bengali (SCB) and ND, drawing the rule partly from Chatterji 1921 on SCB. Haldar's 1929 evidence (initial-vowel lengthening, post-tonic vowel loss in words like ['suiʈka], ['petni]) is word-level. Morshed's ND is Dialect (B), the central (Maijdi) Noakhali variety, from two educated informants aged 27-29 resident in Vancouver.
new_statements.identity_note: Morshed 1972 explicitly describes Dialect (B), the central / Maijdi variety of Noakhali District (informants from 'central part of Noakhali', pp. 17-18); Glottolog's language code for this reference is 'Maijdi Noakhali = Central Noakhali = Noakhali', i.e. the language-level entry noak1234 itself, not one of its dialect children (feni1234 Feni, hati1234 Hatia, etc.). Haldar 1929 describes the mainland Noakhali patois as a whole, distinguishing it from Chittagongese (chit1275), Sandip and the Chandpur/Dacca variety, and his stress section also applies to the district dialect generally. Rashel 2011 covers the Chatkhil (western) sub-dialect and is silent on stress.

The following examples will show the initial stress system of the language.'; sec. 2.53 (p. 50) 'Though word stress is always subsidiary to sentence…
new_statements.relation_note: This is the very source the catalog record and the existing statement were built from; the re-read confirms the quoted sentences, the page numbers (thesis pp. 49-50 = PDF pp. 63-64) and the reading 'fixed: initial syllable' = catalog initial stress. Nothing in the thesis contradicts it. The statement is explicitly about both SCB and ND ('Both in SCB and ND'), so the catalog's ND entry rests on a joint statement rather than an ND-only one.0093434/1 endpoint, and both returned the 4.9 kB 'unusual activity' block page; the copy read is the archive.org user-upload of the same UBC PDF already held by the project ( records both).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is non-contrastive and automatic in both Standard Colloquial Bengali and the Noakhali dialect; it falls on the initial syllable (p. 50: 'always placed on the initial syllable', 'the initial stress system of the language'), and the same page says this initial stressing has caused umlaut and vowel harmony. Word stress is subordinate to sentence stress. Examples given for ND (p. 50): [ˈdʒɔr oiše] 'I got fever', [ˈadʒ ki kirum] 'what shall I do to-day?', [ˈhe balai kam kɔre] 'He got a good job'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing on secondary stress. Sec. 2.51 adds that there are no contrasting levels of stress, and that SCB and ND have an emphatic stress used for emphasis and contrast, realised by tenser consonant articulation and vowel lengthening spreading over a syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: Sec. 2.53 (p. 50): word stress is always subsidiary to sentence stress; conjunctions, particles and auxiliaries in compound verbs receive no stress (citing Chatterjee 1921: 19); a noun following an adjective loses its stress, which falls on the adjective. The p. 50 examples show stress on the first word of the phrase only.
new_statements.identity_note: Morshed's ND corpus comes from two informants (thesis pp. 17-18) 'from the same region (central part of Noakhali, Dialect B)', i.e. the central mainland Maijdi area of Noakhali district, checked against three sailors from the dialect area; the thesis distinguishes three Noakhali sub-dialects (Feni area, Maijdi area, Hatia islands; Fig. 1 and Map 2). The stress statement itself is made jointly for SCB and ND and is partly cited from Chatterjee 1921 (on SCB) and Ferguson and Chowdhury 1960, so it is not an ND-specific finding.

sources.note: Pronunciation notes for the South-Eastern dialect, explicitly 'based on Mr. Pargiter's work' on Chittagong with Noakhali/Hatia additions: 'In words of several syllables, especially those borrowed from Persian or Arabic, the accent is thrown back as far as possible, and the following syllables are lightened.
